clinicalPearls: Coccidian protozoan transmitted by ingesting sporulated oocysts on faecally contaminated fresh produce or water, classically linked to imported berries, salad leaves and herbs
Freshly passed oocysts are not immediately infectious because they require days to sporulate in the environment, so person-to-person spread is negligible
Presents with prolonged, relapsing watery diarrhoea, profound fatigue, anorexia and weight loss, often with a cyclical or remitting-relapsing pattern
Frequently a cause of prolonged traveller's diarrhoea returning from endemic tropical regions
Oocysts are larger than Cryptosporidium and stain variably with modified acid-fast methods, appearing as pink to unstained spheres, and autofluoresce blue-green under ultraviolet light
Cotrimoxazole is the treatment of choice and shortens the otherwise protracted illness
Molecular PCR assays, increasingly part of multiplex gastrointestinal panels, offer sensitive detection when microscopy is negative
reference.pathophysiology: Cyclospora cayetanensis is a coccidian parasite that infects the epithelium of the small intestine. Ingested sporulated oocysts release sporozoites that invade enterocytes, where asexual and sexual cycles generate oocysts excreted unsporulated in the faeces; environmental maturation over days renders them infectious, explaining the food- and water-borne pattern. Mucosal invasion causes villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and inflammation with malabsorption and a secretory diarrhoea. Illness is typically self-limiting in immunocompetent people but can be prolonged and relapsing, and is more severe and persistent when cell-mediated immunity is impaired.
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy with modified acid-fast staining for variably staining oocysts
Ultraviolet autofluorescence microscopy of faecal smears
Molecular PCR or multiplex gastrointestinal panel testing
Repeated stool sampling given intermittent oocyst excretion
Full blood count and assessment of hydration and nutritional status
HIV testing when the illness is prolonged or severe
redFlags: Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from prolonged diarrhoea
Marked weight loss and malabsorption from protracted infection
Severe or unremitting disease suggesting underlying immunosuppression
Cluster of cases pointing to a contaminated food source requiring public health action
reference.prognosis: Self-limiting over weeks in most immunocompetent people but often protracted and relapsing without treatment; antimicrobial therapy produces rapid improvement, while immunocompromised hosts may need extended or suppressive courses.
pitfalls: Failing to request specific stool staining, so oocysts are overlooked on routine microscopy
Attributing persistent traveller's diarrhoea to a purely functional cause without parasitological testing
Assuming person-to-person transmission and missing the food or water source
Under-treating immunocompromised patients who require longer courses
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat with cotrimoxazole as the antimicrobial of choice, which shortens the otherwise protracted, relapsing illness
Use ciprofloxacin as the alternative for patients with sulphonamide intolerance
Provide supportive rehydration, electrolyte correction and attention to nutrition during prolonged diarrhoea and weight loss
In immunocompromised hosts give extended or suppressive courses and optimise antiretroviral therapy where HIV coexists, as relapse is common
Advise food and water hygiene including thorough washing of imported fresh produce to prevent reinfection
Notify public health and support source tracing given the food- and water-borne outbreak pattern
